name: Dave Dell'Aquila
paragraphs: Here’s an early shot of my dad and his Air Force uniform, this was probably taken in the early 1950s

name: Dave Dell'Aquila
paragraphs: Here’s a shot of dad with his beloved 1951 MG TD that he fully restored himself over a number of years. He originally got the car from our family dentist, Dr. Sadler, who told me about it when I was actually having some work done at his office that he had a car that he was going to get rid of, and so I related information to my dad, who ended up acquiring a car and then fully restoring it frame up restoration and did a first class job on it. And one of the funny stories that I have about it is when he was getting the transmission work done, he actually carried the transmission in his briefcase to England and carried it on board and was able to get it through TSA, which didn’t exist at the time, so that was one of the beauties of pre-911 travel.

name: Dave Dell'Aquila
paragraphs: We brought Dad out to fly in a vintage Ford Tri-Motor — and he rode up front, in the cockpit, right beside the pilot.

The airplane behind him, NC9645, is the real thing: a 1928 Ford Tri-Motor — the “City of Wichita” — which helped inaugurate coast-to-coast passenger service in 1929. The Tri-Motor, the corrugated-metal “Tin Goose,” was the airplane that made commercial flight real in America: all-metal, three engines, rugged and dependable enough that airlines built the first transcontinental routes around it, and a nervous public finally trusted flying. Ford built only 199 of them, from 1926 to 1933, and just a handful still fly today.
For a man who wore an Air Force uniform in the early 1950s and spent his life bringing fine machines back to life, there was no better seat in the world.
